Existing surveys, while comprehensive, provide limited guidance for design-to-deployment and seldom re- late fusion quality to task outcomes or device constraints. This work provides a unified perspective that organizes IVIF methods along an interface-attention-alignment coordinate system covering classical spatial/transform pipelines and contemporary deep paradigms (generative, discriminative, multi-task, hybrid/Transformer, dynamic). Wang et al. 1 Introduction Image fusion combines heterogeneous sensor images into a unified representation that enhances scene and object depiction (Meher et al. 2019; Yang et al. 2024). Each modality has distinct strengths and limitations; cross-modal fusion leverages these complementarities to improve resolution, information richness, and interpretability. This benefits both human perception and computer vision tasks such as object detection (Yin et al. 2023), semantic segmentation (Wang et al. 2023), and tracking (Tang et al. 2023). Infrared (IR) imaging remains robust under adverse illumination and weather but typically offers lower spatial detail, whereas visible (VIS) imaging provides richer textures but is illumination-sensitive. Leveraging these cues, IVIF supports applications in transportation, surveillance, recon- naissance, remote sensing, and environmental monitoring. Effective fusion in real-world scenarios is challenging due to environmental noise, sen- sor variability, and cross-modal discrepancies. Rigorous preprocessing-denoising, enhance- ment, and alignment-is therefore required to ensure reliability and complementarity. Successful methods balance information extraction, redundancy minimization, and noise suppression under three guiding principles: consistency, complementarity, and compatibil- ity. Earlier surveys mainly addressed spatial and transform-domain techniques (Yang et al. 2010; Li et al. 2017), with limited coverage of recent deep learning advances or task-driven evaluation. In particular, prior reviews seldom provide systematic comparative analyses, task-driven evaluations, or detailed discussions of generative, discriminative, and multi-task frame- works. To address this gap, our work delivers a comprehensive survey of IVIF methods up to 2025. Representative comparisons with prior high-quality surveys are summarized in Table 1, highlighting differences in time coverage, taxonomy granularity, and emphasis on multi-task, hybrid, robustness, and task-driven evaluation. Contributions. Building on the preceding review, this survey provides a structured and practice-oriented account of IVIF. The main contributions are as follows. (1) We propose a formal taxonomy together with a unified coordinate system along three axes-interfaces, attention & tokenization, and alignment & adaptivity-that integrates traditional spatial/ transform-domain pipelines with contemporary deep paradigms (generative, discrimina- tive, multi-task, hybrid, and composite). (2) We synthesize recent IVIF models (e.g., TD- Fusion (Bai et al. 2025), SAGE-IVIF (Wu et al. 2025) and AMLCA (Wang et al. 2025)) through a systematic comparison of architectural choices, training regimes, and failure modes across datasets and tasks; from this analysis we derive decision criteria that clarify the conditions under which particular designs are preferable. (3) We provide a task- and efficiency-aware reporting protocol, including reference tables that couple fusion metrics with downstream task performance (average precision, AP; mean intersection over union, mIoU) and device-level efficiency (GFLOPs, FPS, memory footprint), thereby enabling commensurable evaluation and facilitating reporting practices that bridge benchmark comparison and deployment. The green arrows indicate how later sections build on earlier building blocks. 2 Traditional fusion methods for image fusion Traditional image fusion methods generally fall into two distinct categories: spatial-domain and transform-domain methods. Spatial-domain methods perform fusion directly on pixel intensities or local features within the original image space, often using weighted averag- ing, principal component analysis (PCA), or filtering-based strategies. Conversely, trans- form-domain methods initially convert images into an alternative representation before performing fusion, with representative examples including image pyramid methods, wave- let transforms, and more advanced designs such as curvelet and contourlet transforms. Each category leverages domain-specific prior knowledge, offering foundational strategies that enhance image fusion by addressing complementary aspects of image information integration. Despite their foundational significance, traditional fusion methods exhibit critical limita- tions that reduce their effectiveness in contemporary applications. One significant issue is their heavy reliance on manual expertise and domain-specific experience, leading to inher- ently inflexible and complex algorithms that often struggle with intricate or nuanced image features. Furthermore, these methods have limited capacity for feature extraction, predomi- nantly relying on handcrafted pixel-level or local-region features, which inadequately rep- resent high-level semantic information. As a result, their performance degrades notably in complex or varied scenarios, driving researchers to pursue more robust and adaptive solu- tions, notably through deep learning techniques. These approaches typically follow a pipeline involv- ing image registration, region partitioning, weight estimation, and final reconstruction. For example, methods like Support Vector Machine (SVM) (Li et al. 2004), neural networks (Li et al. 2002), and Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) (Liu et al. 2015) design simple weight measurement networks to process pixel values and perform superposition or rearrangement at the pixel level. Before applying the weighted algorithm, generating an accurate weight map is essential, with the primary differences among these methods lying in their pixel fusion techniques. Commonly used methods include the maximum (or averag- ing, minimum) pixel value technique, weighted averaging method, PCA algorithm, IHS, and guided filtering. PCA is a widely used method for spectral-space transformation in image fusion. For instance, Shahdoosti and Ghassemian (2016) proposed a data transformation technique that applies PCA separately to the spatial information of neighboring pixels and the spectral domain, combining both results to fuse multimodal images. Since PCA calculates its coef- ficients based on the statistical properties of the data, this method is highly adaptable and robust. Building upon this idea, Li et al. Recent spatial-domain fusion methods typically start by estimating an initial weight map using differences in brightness and color (Li and Kang 2012), then refine this estimation through techniques such as image matting (Li et al. 2013). To further enhance results, they often apply recursive filtering for a coarse-to-fine refinement of the fused image (Gastal and Oliveira 2011). These initial weight estimation and refinement steps lay the groundwork for a structured pipeline commonly adopted by spatial-domain fusion techniques. In fact, most spatial-domain fusion approaches generally follow a standardized workflow. First, image registration aligns the source images geometrically through transformations like translation, rotation, and scaling, ensuring precise pixel correspondence. Subsequently, preprocessing operations, including grayscale conversion and noise reduction, enhance image quality. Once preprocessed, the segmentation stage partitions the images into distinct regions based on features such as texture, content, and color. Fusion rule design then creates tailored fusion criteria for each region by assessing pixel intensity, texture, and structural details. Region-level fusion applies these rules carefully, emphasizing smooth transitions at boundaries to ensure visual consistency. The process concludes with post-processing and optimization steps, such as sharpening and edge enhancement, refining the overall image quality. While spatial-domain methods directly manipulate pixel values, providing advantages such as computational efficiency and ease of implementation, their effectiveness remains highly sensitive to the accuracy of pixel weight estimations. For instance, some techniques employ weighted averaging guided by pixel activity levels (Gangapure et al. 2015), while others integrate wavelet coefficients and SVM-based feature classification for fusion tasks (Yu et al. 2016). Despite these varied strategies, pixel- or neighborhood-level approaches frequently neglect correlations between neighboring pixels, prompting the adoption of region-based fusion methods. However, even region-based methods, which segment images and fuse regions individually, can introduce noticeable block artifacts at region boundaries and rely significantly on accurate segmentation results. Furthermore, classical spatial-domain methods largely depend on handcrafted fusion rules for allocating pixel weights, thereby lacking semantic awareness and adaptability to image content. Consequently, they exhibit limited robustness in complex scenes, particu- larly when faced with inaccuracies in segmentation, resulting in artifacts or smoothing out critical local details. These shortcomings become more evident in challenging scenarios involving low-contrast images, occlusion, and significant background clutter, ultimately restricting their applicability and scalability in diverse real-world contexts. 2.1.2 Advanced strategies To further elaborate on these traditional approaches and their advancements, we next dis- cuss several sophisticated spatial-domain techniques, such as saliency-driven fusion, gradi- ent-energy-based fusion, and edge-preserving filtering. Practical deployment therefore calls for condition-aware fusion that adapts modality contributions rather than relying on fixed rules. Dynamic fusion re-weights IR/VIS signals over time and space via attention, gating, or lightweight controllers embedded in Transformer backbones and CNN–Transformer hybrids. Diag- nosis relates temporal weights and alignment quality to measurable factors (flow magni- tude, occlusion masks, exposure change), checking monotonic responses-greater motion or occlusion should increase reliance on aligned features or conservative gating. Multi-task learning (MTL) offers a principled route by coupling low-level fusion quality with high-level semantics within a unified objective. Effective MTL frameworks typically share an encoder across fusion and task heads while preserving task-specific capacity (e.g., decoupled heads or lightweight adapters). Joint opti- mization aligns features to task objectives, and adaptive loss weighting balances compet- ing criteria as scenes vary. Attention-guided heads can steer fusion toward task-relevant structures (targets, edges, anomalies), while causal probes test whether learned interactions genuinely support decisions. Evaluation should couple qualitative evidence with quantitative summaries that reveal alignment between fusion and tasks. Visualization: overlay activation or attention maps from task heads on fused images to verify emphasis on task-critical regions across condi- tions. Diagnosis: correlate task metrics with fusion indicators to expose trade-offs and fail- ure modes (e.g., high SSIM but low detection accuracy). Quantification: report joint curves of fusion quality versus task accuracy and summarize multi-objective trade-offs (e.g., Pareto fronts over accuracy, latency, and memory) to make efficiency–utility compromises explicit. Recommendations. 1. Adopt joint objectives that directly link fusion quality to downstream performance, and use adaptive loss balancing to stabilize optimization across conditions. 2. Use task-aware interpretability: tie attribution/saliency from task heads to decision out- comes so that explanations reflect operational utility. 3. Establish causal evaluation protocols (counterfactuals, ablations) to verify that fused information-rather than spurious cues-drives task gains. 4. Standardize multi-objective reporting with joint curves and Pareto fronts so that accu- racy–efficiency–stability trade-offs are comparable across models and datasets. 6.7 Cross-modal foundation models Large-scale pretrained cross-modal models provide unified backbones with broad repre- sentational capacity. Although most were developed for vision–language objectives, their feature abstractions and alignment priors are applicable to infrared–visible (IR–VIS) fusion, where spectral discrepancy, misregistration, and domain shift are prevalent. Integrating such backbones offers a path to improved generalization and reduced reliance on task-specific retraining, provided that adaptation and efficiency are carefully controlled. Adoption in IVIF is constrained by three factors: computational cost, distribution mis- match between pretraining corpora and operational data, and the need for real-time or embedded deployment. When streaming is required, state management and causal execution must be explicit to bound delay and stabilize behavior. Wang et al. 7 Conclusion This survey synthesized infrared–visible image fusion (IVIF) across classical spatial/ transform pipelines and modern transformer, hybrid, and dynamic architectures under an interface–attention–alignment perspective. We introduced a comparison-to-deployment protocol that couples fusion and task metrics with device-level latency/memory and condi- tion–performance curves. Empirically, classical methods are lightweight and interpretable yet sensitive to misregistration and adverse capture; pure transformers preserve structure at higher cost; CNN–Transformer hybrids balance accuracy and efficiency; dynamic rout- ing improves resilience in nonstationary settings; and video fusion benefits from causal memory with motion/flow-aware alignment. Foundation backbones are promising but need parameter-efficient adaptation and compression for embedded use. We expect the taxonomy and protocol to support reproducible, resource-aware deployments. Strengths. (i) A unified taxonomy enabling like-for-like comparison across classical, transformer-based, hybrid, and dynamic families; (ii) a deployment-facing evaluation pro- tocol pairing fusion and task utility with latency/memory and condition-aware robustness; (iii) explicit treatment of temporal consistency, misregistration, and adverse-capture deg- radation; (iv) practical guidance linking alignment/attention and token/window control to engineering constraints. Weaknesses. (i) Video fusion remains under-benchmarked, with limited public long- sequence baselines and temporal metrics; (ii) efficiency reports (FPS, memory, energy) are partly literature-sourced and not strictly comparable across hardware/precision; (iii) secu- rity (adversarial/spoofing) and radiometric calibration receive limited coverage; (iv) niche/ domain-specific pipelines are necessarily brief due to space and data availability. Implications. Progress hinges on multi-dimensional reporting-accuracy, robustness, interpretability, and efficiency-rather than single-score optimization. Standardized temporal and robustness protocols, coupled with parameter-efficient adaptation of cross-modal back- bones, will tighten the loop between laboratory results and field reliability and lower the barrier to embedded deployment. Recommendations. 1) Reporting: pair fusion metrics with downstream task scores, latency/FPS, memory, and condition–performance curves; include calibration/uncertainty. 2) Robustness: train and audit with degradation ladders (misregistration, low-light, weather, noise) and report worst-case and cross-domain gaps. 3) Video: use causal memory with motion/flow-aware alignment; report temporal SSIM/ghosting and release scripts. 4) Inter- pretability: provide attention/Grad-CAM and concept-based analyses aligned with sensor physics; assess explanation consistency across conditions. 5) Efficiency: adopt adapters/ LoRA, distillation, and quantization; control tokens/windows and measure on-device mem- ory/energy beyond FLOPs. 6) Data & Benchmarks: curate balanced day/night and adverse- weather sets with registration-quality indicators; tie fusion to detection/segmentation labels; release configs/seeds/hardware/precision for reproducibility. JSON: Name: align_diffuse_fuse Title: Conditional diffusion-transformer fusion with pre-attention deformable alignment and task-aware supervision for robust infrared-visible image fusion Short Hypothesis: Integrating a pre-attention deformable alignment module and a conditional diffusion-transformer fusion network trained with a joint fusion+task loss will increase object detection mAP@0.5 by at least 5 percentage points and semantic segmentation mIoU by at least 3 percentage points on the M3FD test set under controlled misregistration (±10 pixels) and noise (Gaussian σ=10) relative to the best-performing baseline SwinFusion. Related Work: Prior infrared-visible image fusion approaches include classical spatial and transform pipelines (pyramid, wavelet, DCT/FFT, NSCT/NSST) and sparse-representation/hybrid methods that explicitly separate frequency bands. Deep-learning methods split into discriminative (CNN/autoencoder) models that are efficient but limited in global context, generative adversarial networks that produce visually realistic outputs but suffer training instability, and diffusion-based generative models that yield stable high-fidelity sampling at high computational cost. Transformer-based and CNN–Transformer hybrids address long-range cross-modal dependencies but are memory- and data-intensive. Joint multi-task fusion integrates detection/segmentation objectives to align fused outputs with downstream tasks but raises optimization and compute complexity. Existing approaches commonly suffer from (1) sensitivity to cross-modal misregistration and parallax, (2) lack of standardized condition-aware robustness evaluation, (3) limited temporal consistency for video, (4) metric–task mismatch where pixel-level gains do not translate to task gains, and (5) deployment impracticality due to high latency or memory footprint. No prior method combines pre-attention deformable alignment, conditional diffusion sampling, transformer global context, and explicit task supervision in a single, deployment-aware pipeline. Abstract: We propose a modular infrared-visible image fusion method that combines pre-attention deformable alignment, conditional diffusion-based synthesis, and transformer-mediated cross-modal fusion trained under joint fusion and downstream-task supervision. The method first estimates and applies deformable warping at feature level to correct parallax and local misregistration prior to attention. A conditional diffusion denoiser operates in a tokenized transformer latent space to iteratively reconstruct fused imagery while a lightweight task head (object detection or semantic segmentation) provides task-specific gradients during training. The main contribution is the integration of alignment, probabilistic generative sampling, global attention, and task-aware loss into a single pipeline with explicit condition-performance evaluation. Expected outcomes are (i) improved robustness to misregistration, noise, and low-light degradations, (ii) measurable improvements in detection and segmentation metrics under perturbation, and (iii) a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol reporting latency, memory, and condition–performance curves. Experiments: Datasets: M3FD (use 80% train, 10% val, 10% test stratified by scene type), MSRS (80/10/10), RoadScene (80/10/10), LLVIP (use test splits for low-light evaluation), TNO (subset for night/fog cases), MFNet (cross-dataset generalization). Baselines: DenseFuse, SwinFusion, CDDFuse, DDFM (diffusion baseline), FusionGAN, SegMiF (task-aware baseline), TarDAL (target-aware adversarial), and a no-alignment ablation of SwinFusion. Metrics: fusion-quality MI, Qabf, VIF, SSIM, AG, SF; downstream detection: AP@0.5 and mAP@0.5:0.95 using YOLOv8; segmentation: mIoU and per-class IoU using SegFormer-B5; temporal: tSSIM and temporal LPIPS on video subsets; robustness: condition–performance curves under misregistration/noise/weather; compute: GFLOPs@input, parameter count, peak GPU memory, latency (mean, P50, P95) measured on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 with FP16 inference. Perturbations: geometric misregistration offsets sampled uniformly in {±0, ±5, ±10, ±20} pixels and elastic jitter magnitudes; photometric noise Gaussian σ∈{0,5,10,20}; fog/haze simulated with scattering density ∈{0.0,0.25,0.5,0.75}; low-light brightness scale factors ∈{1.0,0.6,0.3,0.1}. Training setup: train proposed model end-to-end with 2-stage regime: (a) pretrain alignment+transformer encoder for 50 epochs, (b) train full conditional diffusion+task head for 100 epochs; optimizer AdamW, lr=1e-4 with cosine decay, batch size 8, mixed-precision AMP. Ablation studies: (1) remove pre-attention deformable alignment, (2) replace diffusion with deterministic UNet decoder, (3) remove task loss (fusion-only), (4) replace transformer tokens with patch-CNN tokens, (5) compare conditional diffusion with GAN and with teacher-student distilled diffusion. Comparisons: evaluate each model on clean and perturbed test splits; report mean±std over 3 random seeds; perform paired t-tests against SwinFusion for detection mAP and segmentation mIoU, significance level α=0.05. Deployment profiling: measure throughput and memory under tiled inference (tile sizes 512 and 1024 with 64-pixel overlap) and with INT8 quantized student model. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes include (1) pre-attention deformable alignment failing for large parallax or non-Lambertian surfaces, producing residual ghosting; (2) conditional diffusion sampling incurring high inference latency and memory usage that prevent real-time deployment; (3) diffusion or transformer components hallucinating modality-specific textures, causing modality dominance and misleading downstream decisions; (4) joint task supervision causing negative transfer where task gradients degrade fusion fidelity under mismatched objectives. Data and evaluation biases: training datasets may underrepresent certain weather, camera spectral responses, or sensor calibrations, limiting generalization to unseen sensors or extreme environments. Scalability and compute limits: end-to-end diffusion-transformer pipelines require large GPU memory and long training times, hindering hyperparameter sweeps and large-scale pretraining. Limits to generalization: performance gains established on selected benchmarks may not transfer to long video sequences with rolling-shutter artifacts or to domains with severe radiometric differences (e.g., thermal reflections), and improvements under modest perturbation ranges may not hold under extreme misregistration/noise beyond tested perturbation ladders.
